title: You're Not Busy. You're Hiding.
author: By Title Only
summary: The author argues that chronic busyness in leaders is often a sophisticated avoidance strategy — a socially acceptable way to defer the hardest, most consequential work by filling the calendar with activity that feels productive but avoids real risk. Using the example of a perpetually overbooked VP, the article shows how busyness creates the appearance of leadership contribution while masking strategic avoidance of difficult decisions. The kayak question is introduced as a diagnostic: if you circumnavigated the world by kayak with no communications, which calendar items would still move forward without you? The gap between what would continue and what would stall reveals which activities are genuinely necessary versus which exist to make the leader feel useful. The article concludes that addressing chronic busyness requires confronting the discomfort driving the avoidance — the harder work that keeps getting deferred.
points: Chronic busyness in leaders is often a socially acceptable avoidance strategy — a way to appear productive while deferring the hardest, most consequential work.
The calendar of a chronically busy leader is frequently an accurate map of what they are avoiding rather than what they are genuinely accomplishing.
If you circumnavigated the world by kayak with no communications devices, which items on your calendar would still move forward without you?
The gap between what would continue and what would stall reveals which activities are truly necessary and which exist primarily to make the leader feel useful.
Addressing busyness requires confronting the underlying discomfort driving the avoidance — the work that keeps getting deferred because it is genuinely hard.
quotes: If you decided tomorrow to circumnavigate the world by kayak — no phone, no laptop, no opportunity to send your team a quick thought, nothing to do but keep paddling and don’t get eaten by the sharks — what on your calendar would still move forward in a good enough way without you?
And of course there’s always that conversation you keep rescheduling because the timing isn’t quite right — which is fascinating, because apparently the right time is a day after never.
So I asked Sharon: “If we looked at everything on your calendar this week, how many of the things are actually moving you closer towards your goals?” She paused for a while.
The Con Job You see, we’ve somehow decided that being too busy to think is proof that you’re important, instead of proof that something has gone really deeply sideways.
And there’s just enough pride in the way she says it to make me think she doesn’t mean it the way I would expect her to mean it.
And you can end the day completely exhausted and point to that exhaustion as proof that you actually accomplished something.
We’re gonna call her Sharon — because I love the show Catastrophe and was just talking about Sharon Horgan this morning.
